title: Synonyms & Antonyms
summary: One synonym and one antonym in a typical Tier 1 shift — two fast marks that reward a word bank, not guesswork. The root-word method decodes unknown words; degree and charge matching settle the rest. Below: 100 high-frequency synonyms and 60 antonyms with meanings, written for revision in daily 15-minute doses.

subtopics.title: The root-word method: decode words you have never seen
subtopics.concept:
SSC vocabulary questions recycle the same few thousand words, but every year a couple of words are new to almost everyone. The root-word method converts such words from guesses into deductions: most English 'hard' words are built from Latin and Greek parts, and knowing 40 roots covers hundreds of exam words.

| Root | Sense | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| bene- | good, well | benevolent, benefit, benign, benefactor |
| mal-/male- | bad | malevolent, malice, malfunction, malnutrition |
| bon-/eu- | good | bona fide, euphoria, eulogy |
| loqu / locut | speak | eloquent, loquacious, elocution, soliloquy |
| dict | say, declare | dictate, contradict, verdict, predict |
| voc / vok | call, voice | vocal, revoke, advocate, invoke |
| cred | believe | credible, credulous, incredible, credit |
| mit / miss | send | transmit, emissary, remit, missile |
| path | feeling, suffering | sympathy, apathy, empathy, pathological |
| sens / sent | feel | sensitive, sentiment, consensus, dissent |
| morph | shape, form | amorphous, metamorphosis, morpheme |
| chron | time | chronic, chronology, synchronise, anachronism |
| temp | time | temporary, contemporary, temporal |
| ego | self | egocentric, egoist, alter ego |
| ambi / amphi | both, around | ambiguous, ambidextrous, amphibious |
| am / amic | love, friend | amiable, amicable, amity, amorous |
| anthrop | human | anthropology, philanthropy, misanthrope |
| phil | love | philanthropy, philosopher, bibliophile |
| phob | fear | phobia, hydrophobia, acrophobia |
| gen | birth, kind | genius, generate, genocide, congenital |
| graph / scrib / script | write | autograph, describe, manuscript, scribble |
| spec / spect | look | inspect, spectator, circumspect, perspective |
| vis / vid | see | visible, evident, vision, provident |
| aud | hear | audible, audience, auditorium |
| port | carry | transport, portable, export, deport |
| duc / duct | lead | conduct, educate, deduce, aqueduct |
|  tract | pull, draw | attract, extract, retract, tractable |
| press | press, push | compress, depress, impression |
| pos / pon | place | position, postpone, deposit, component |
| sequ / secut | follow | sequence, consequence, execute, sequel |
| cert | sure | certain, certify, ascertain |
| cur / curs | run | current, excursion, cursory, cursive |
| rupt | break | rupture, interrupt, bankrupt, erupt |
| fid | faith | confide, fidelity, diffident, confident |
| greg | flock, group | gregarious, segregate, aggregate |
| jur / jud | law, judge | jury, justice, prejudice, adjudicate |
| leg / lex | law, read | legal, legislate, legacy, lexicon |
| sol | alone / sun | solitude, solitary, solo / solar, solstice |
| ver | truth | verify, veracity, verdict, veritable |
| grad / gress | step, go | gradual, progress, digress, egress |

**How to deploy it in the exam.** When you meet an unknown word, split it:
- *MALEVOLENT* = male- (bad) + vol (wish) + -ent → 'wishing bad' → hostile. Even without recalling *vol*, 'male-' alone rules out friendly options.
- *CIRCUMSPECT* = circum- (around) + spect (look) → 'looking around' → cautious.
- *SOLILOQUY* = soli (alone) + loqu (speak) → 'speaking alone' → a monologue.

Prefixes and suffixes also reveal the part of speech even when meaning stays dark: *-ous/-ful* build adjectives (*dangerous*), *-tion/-ment* build nouns (*creation*), *-ise/-fy* build verbs (*simplify*). Knowing the class alone eliminates two of four options in synonym questions, because options usually mix classes.

**Build the habit:** whenever you learn a new word, spend ten seconds finding its root. The root then pays out on every relative of that word — learn *credulous* and *incredible, credible, creed, credential* all come free.

tricks.title: Split-then-eliminate
tricks.body: Chop the unknown word at its joins (bene-vol-ent), translate the parts you know, and eliminate options contradicting them. One confident root kills two options.

example.q: BENEVOLENT means: cruel / kindly / generous-sized / talkative.
example.solution: *Bene-* = good → the kind option. *Malevolent* (male- = bad) would be the antonym — options often plant it as a decoy.

tricks.title: Family clustering
tricks.body: Learn words in root families, not alphabetical order: dict family (dictate, verdict, indomitable? no — edict, indict), loqu family (eloquent, loquacious). One sitting per family.

tricks.title: Positive/negative split
tricks.body: Roots carry emotional charge: bene-, eu-, am- are warm; mal-, dys-, phob-, mis- are cold. When stuck, mark the word's charge and choose an option of matching charge.

mistakes: Trusting the first familiar half ('understand' contains 'stand' but is not about standing).
Ignoring suffixes and losing the part-of-speech elimination.
Learning alphabetical lists; root families stick, alphabet lists evaporate.
subtopics.notes:
### Why roots work
A synonym question gives you a word and four options. When you do not know the word, you are not helpless: most hard exam words are built from **prefix + root + suffix**, and the same few dozen parts appear again and again. Decode the parts, and you can often choose the nearest meaning without ever having seen the word.

### The prefixes that appear most
| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| in-, im-, il-, ir-, un-, dis- | not | indispensable (cannot be done without), illegible, irregular |
| mal- | bad | malicious, malnutrition |
| bene- | good, well | benefactor, benevolent |
| circum- | around | circumvent, circumference |
| pre-, post- | before, after | postpone, precaution |
| sub-, super- | under, above | subordinate, supervise |
| mono-, poly- | one, many | monotone, polyglot |
| auto- | self | autobiography, autograph |
| magn- | great | magnanimous, magnitude |
| chron- | time | chronological, chronicle |
| aud-, vis-, spect- | hear, see, look | audible, visible, inspect |
| port- | carry | portable, transport |
| dict- | say | dictate, contradict |
| tract- | pull | attract, extract |
| anim- | mind, spirit | magnanimous, unanimous |

### The method, step by step
1. **Split the word** into parts you recognise: MAGNANIMOUS = magn (great) + anim (mind, spirit) + ous (adjective ending).
2. **Translate the parts**: great-spirited → generous, ready to forgive.
3. **Match with the options**: generous is the nearest meaning.
4. **Check the part of speech**: -ous, -ful, -ive endings usually mean an adjective; -tion, -ment, -ness a noun. Your answer should match.

### When the method misleads: the false-root trap
A few famous words *look* like they contain a helpful root, but the meaning has drifted. Learn these five as fixed exceptions:
- **enervate** = to weaken (it looks like 'energy' but means the opposite).
- **restive** = restless, hard to control (it looks like 'rest' = calm).
- **inflammable** = easily set on fire (it does not mean 'not flammable').
- **invaluable** = extremely valuable (it does not mean 'worthless').
- **noisome** = foul-smelling (it has nothing to do with noise).

If you know the word directly, trust your memory over the root. Use the root only as a *guessing* tool for unknown words, and be extra careful when an option simply repeats the root's surface meaning — for enervate, the trap option is 'to energise'.

### Building speed
In practice, run a two-second prefix check on every option: *does its prefix match the stem word's prefix family?* If the stem has a positive prefix (bene-) and an option carries a negative one (mal-), the option is almost certainly wrong. This one habit removes one or two options in most questions even when you do not know any word fully.

### Quick revision
- Split → translate → match → check part of speech.
- Core prefixes: not (in/im/il/ir/un/dis), bad (mal), good (bene), around (circum), one/many (mono/poly), self (auto), before/after (pre/post).
- Core roots: spect (look), port (carry), dict (say), chron (time), anim (spirit), tract (pull), aud (hear).
- Memorise the false-root five: enervate, restive, inflammable, invaluable, noisome.

patterns.name: Prefix gives the direction (positive or negative)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem word starts with a strong prefix (mal-, bene-, in-/un-/dis-) and one or two options start with opposite prefixes.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the prefix: mal = bad, bene = good, in/un/dis = not.
2. Fix the direction of the meaning before reading the options.
3. Reject options whose direction clashes; choose the nearest positive/negative match.

*Why it works:* prefixes are stable across thousands of words.

example.solution: mal = bad → intending harm → **spiteful**. Kind-hearted fails the direction check.

patterns.name: Root gives the core meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The stem contains a root you know (spect, port, dict, chron, anim) even if the whole word is unfamiliar.
patterns.logic:
1. Strip the prefix and suffix; find the root.
2. Recall the root's meaning (port = carry, chron = time).
3. Pick the option built on that core idea.

*Why it works:* Greek and Latin roots keep their meaning in every English word that borrows them.

example.solution: magn (great) + anim (spirit) → **generous, forgiving**.

patterns.name: Chunking a long word into known pieces
patterns.howToSpot: The word is long and technical-looking (chronological, indispensable, circumvent).
patterns.logic:
1. Cut the word where a known piece ends: circum + vent.
2. Translate piece by piece: around + come.
3. Assemble: to come around → to get around a rule by cleverness.

*Why it works:* long exam words are usually transparent stacks of two known pieces.

example.solution: chron = time → arranged in time order. Alphabetical is the planted wrong order.

patterns.name: False-root trap words
patterns.howToSpot: An option simply repeats the surface root (energise for enervate, calm for restive, worthless for invaluable).
patterns.logic:
1. Check the word against the memorised false-root list first.
2. If it is on the list, ignore the apparent root and use the fixed meaning.
3. Then treat the root-repeating option as the trap, not the answer.

*Why it works:* these five words are famous precisely because their shape misleads.

example.solution: **Weaken**, not energise. The 'energy' shape is the trap.

subtopics.title: Choosing the nearest meaning: elimination by class, degree, charge
subtopics.concept:
A synonym question asks for the word closest in meaning. Options are engineered around three axes — fix them in order:

**1. Part of speech.** Decide whether the given word is a noun, verb or adjective; options that are not the same class are out immediately. *AFFECT* (verb) cannot have 'affection' (noun) as a synonym even though it looks closest.

**2. Degree.** The nearest synonym matches the *intensity*. *WEARY* (very tired) is closer to *exhausted* than to *tired*; *FUTILE* (completely fruitless) is closer to *pointless* than to *difficult*. When two options both fit, take the one at the same temperature.

**3. Connotation and register.** A word's emotional colour must match. *NOTORIOUS* (famous for bad reasons) pairs with *infamous*, not with *celebrated*, even though both mean 'widely known'. *SLIM* and *skinny* both mean thin, but *slim* is approving and *skinny* is not — synonym options are chosen across this line.

**Practical routine for 20 seconds:**
1. Say the given word's meaning in your own simple words.
2. Translate each option into its own simple meaning.
3. Keep the option whose simple meaning overlaps most — overlap, not association. (*Cinema* associates with *film* but is not its synonym.)

**No sentence is given in SSC's format** — so context cannot rescue you. This is the one topic where the answer must be known, which is exactly why the word banks in this topic deserve daily 15-minute revision rather than a single reading.

tricks.title: Overlap test
tricks.body: The right synonym shares the core idea, not the neighbourhood. Ask 'can one replace the other in most sentences?' — if the sentence changes meaning, it is an associate, not a synonym.

example.solution: *Eloquent* = speaking fluently and movingly = **articulate**. 'Quiet' is a near-antonym planted for sound-alike confusion.

tricks.title: Charge matching
tricks.body: Label the given word + or − (notorious −, celebrated +) and pick the option of the same sign. Half of synonym options fall to charge alone.

tricks.title: Degree ruler
tricks.body: Place the word and both surviving options on an intensity line (mild → extreme). The option at the same mark is the answer.

mistakes: Choosing the option that merely sounds academic ('utilise' is fine, but 'effectuate' for 'do' is not SSC's style).
Picking a word of the wrong part of speech that shares a root with the answer.
Forgetting the negative flip: 'famous for good deeds' ≠ notorious.
subtopics.notes:
### You rarely need the exact word
A synonym question asks for the **nearest** meaning. You do not have to recall a dictionary definition; you only have to remove three options that are wrong in an obvious way. Options are built to fail on one of four filters, so run the filters in order.

### Filter 1: part of speech
Decide what the stem word is: ADAPTABLE ends in -able (adjective), ABOLISH is a verb, ABOLITION a noun.
- An adjective answer should be an adjective or adjective phrase.
- Trap: for the verb RELEASE, the noun 'freedom' is planted. It is related but not a match in part of speech.
If an option is a different part of speech, remove it unless no better option remains.

### Filter 2: class or family
The nearest meaning must belong to the **same class of idea**.
- DELUGE (a flood of water) → drizzle, drought and mist are all water or weather words, but only *flood* shares the class 'a large amount of water'.
- Remove options from a different class first: for DELUGE, an option like 'quarrel' dies instantly.

### Filter 3: degree
Within the right class, match the strength.
- TRIVIAL = of very little importance. 'Serious' and 'vital' are importance words of the wrong degree; the answer sits at the *low* end.
- ENORMOUS = huge; a mild word like 'big' is usually too weak when the stem has an extreme word.
If the stem word is extreme (enormous, furious, exhausted), the answer is normally extreme too.

### Filter 4: charge (positive or negative)
Note whether the word is pleasant or unpleasant:
- NOTORIOUS = famous for something bad → the answer must be negative (infamous), so 'well known' alone is not enough.
- HOSTILE, timid, generous, warm — each carries a charge. Keep only options with the same charge.

### If a sentence is given
Some papers print the word inside a sentence. The sentence overrides everything: SPEED can mean 'hurry' in one sentence and 'fastness' in another. Read the sentence, decide what the word does *there*, then match. Never answer from the word's most common meaning alone when a context is supplied.

### Order of operations in the exam
1. Say the stem word's meaning to yourself in one plain word.
2. Part of speech — remove mismatches.
3. Class — remove unrelated ideas.
4. Degree and charge — remove the survivors that are too weak or wrongly toned.
5. Choose the remaining option and read it back: "X means about the same as Y" should sound true.

### Quick revision
- Four filters in order: part of speech → class → degree → charge.
- Extreme stem word → extreme answer.
- NOTORIOUS is negative; its answer must be negative.
- With a sentence, the context meaning wins over the dictionary meaning.
- You need the *nearest*, not the perfect, match.

patterns.name: Part-of-speech filter
patterns.howToSpot: Among the options one is a noun where the stem is a verb (or similar mismatch), often a related word like freedom for RELEASE.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the stem's part of speech from its ending and its use.
2. Remove options of a different part of speech.
3. Choose among the survivors.

*Why it works:* a synonym must be replaceable in the same sentence slot.

example.solution: Verb → **set free**. 'Freedom' is the same family but a noun — the planted trap.

patterns.name: Degree match
patterns.howToSpot: Two options share the right class but differ in strength (serious vs vital vs unimportant for TRIVIAL).
patterns.logic:
1. Place the stem word on its scale (weak — strong; small — huge).
2. Note whether it sits at an extreme.
3. Pick the option at the same position on the scale.

*Why it works:* nearest meaning means nearest in strength too.

example.solution: Low importance → **unimportant**. Serious and vital sit at the wrong end.

patterns.name: Charge (tone) match
patterns.howToSpot: The stem is clearly positive or negative (hostile, notorious, generous), and one option has the right idea but the wrong tone.
patterns.logic:
1. Label the stem + or -.
2. Label each surviving option + or -.
3. Keep only options with the same label.

*Why it works:* a positive word can never be the nearest meaning of a negative one.

example.solution: Negative → **unfriendly**. Calm and shy are not the charge of an enemy.

patterns.name: Meaning from the sentence context
patterns.howToSpot: The word appears in CAPITALS inside a sentence, and the options are possible meanings.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the whole sentence and say what the capitalised word does there.
2. Ignore other meanings you know for that word.
3. Match the sentence meaning to one option.

*Why it works:* the examiner keys the answer to the context, not the dictionary.

example.q: *His reply was LACONIC — just two words.*
example.solution: Two-word reply → **using very few words**.

subtopics.title: Antonyms: prefix flips and real opposites
subtopics.concept:
An antonym is a word opposite in meaning. Two skills cover SSC antonym questions.

**Skill 1 — the opposite, not the absence.** The correct antonym reverses the meaning; it does not merely differ. For *BRAVE* the antonym is *cowardly*, not *careful*. For *PRAISE* it is *criticise*, not *ignore* — ignoring is not the opposite of praising. Test each option by making a mini-sentence pair: 'He praised the plan / He criticised the plan' — clean contradiction.

**Skill 2 — build the flip.** Most adjectives flip with a prefix:

| Prefix | Effect | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| un- | not / reverse | unfair, unwell, undo, untie |
| in- / im- / il- / ir- | not | inactive, impossible, illogical, irregular |
| dis- | opposite, apart | disagree, disorder, disconnect, discredit |
| non- | not | nonsense, nonstop, nonviolent |
| mis- | wrongly | misjudge, misplace, misinterpret |
| de- | down, reverse | decrease, deflate, decompose |
| anti- | against | antisocial, antidote, antiseptic |
| counter- | against, opposite | counteract, counterclaim |
| -less | without | harmless, restless, speechless |
| -ful / -ous | full of (builds the positive) | harmful, dangerous, famous |

Prefix knowledge works in both directions: meet *irreversible*, know it means *reversible* negated; need the opposite of *conformity*, answer *nonconformity* or *defiance*. Watch the four-way *in- / im- / il- / ir-* spelling split — it follows the next sound (impossible, illegal, irregular) and decides spelling questions as a bonus.

**Antonym families to bank together:** agree/disagree, appear/disappear, increase/decrease, superior/inferior, permanent/temporary, expand/contract, vacant/occupied, sacred/profane, native/foreign, optimist/pessimist. SSC antonyms usually come straight from these families.

**Degree opposites:** gradable pairs sit on one line — hot↔cold, abundant↔scarce, shallow↔deep. Complementary pairs allow no middle — alive↔dead, guilty↔innocent. Both types appear; recognising the type prevents choosing a merely-different word.

tricks.title: Mini-sentence contradiction
tricks.body: Put the word and each candidate in the same short sentence ('The manager praised / criticised the report'). The option producing a genuine contradiction is the antonym.

example.q: Antonym of CORDIAL: warm / polite / hostile / sincere.
example.solution: 'A cordial welcome' ↔ 'a hostile welcome' — real opposites. 'Polite' and 'sincere' can coexist with cordial, so neither contradicts it.

tricks.title: Prefix flip check
tricks.body: Before scanning options, guess the flip yourself (conformity → nonconformity). If your guess is among the options, mark it — the options are built around the same flip.

tricks.title: Absence is not opposition
tricks.body: Kill options that merely lack the quality ('careful' for 'brave'). An antonym fights the word; it does not stand beside it.

mistakes: Choosing a word from a different part of speech ('arrive' as antonym of 'departure').
Taking a near-neutral word ('polite') as the opposite of a warm word ('cordial').
Opposing the wrong sense of a polysemous word ('fresh' = new vs unwilted; SSC picks the listed sense).
subtopics.notes:
### What 'most opposite' really asks
An antonym question gives a word and asks for the option **furthest** from it in meaning. Two words can both be unrelated to the stem; only one is its true opposite. Your job is to recognise which kind of opposite the exam wants.

### Three kinds of opposite
1. **Complementary** — one or the other, nothing between: alive / dead, present / absent, accept / refuse.
2. **Gradable** — two ends of a scale: hot / cold, maximum / minimum, abundant / scarce, minor / major.
3. **Direction or role** — opposite movements or roles: buy / sell, ascend / descend, employer / employee, immigrate / emigrate.

Before looking at the options, decide the kind: it stops you from choosing a merely *different* word.

### The prefix-flip trap
The most common wrong option is a word that **looks** opposite because of its prefix but actually means the same as the stem:
- **invaluable** = extremely valuable (so its opposite is worthless, and 'valuable' is the trap).
- **inflammable** = easily set on fire (opposite: fireproof; 'flammable' means the same, not the opposite).
- **disinterested** = impartial (not 'uninterested').
- **restive** = restless (not calm).
Rule: never build the opposite by sticking a prefix on the stem word. Know the stem's real meaning first, then find its opposite.

### The synonym trap
Every antonym question also carries at least one **synonym** of the stem among the options. For SUPERFLUOUS (more than needed), the options include extra and surplus — both mean the same as the stem. Learn to laugh at them: in an antonym question, a synonym option is always wrong. This one observation usually removes two of the four options immediately.

### Keep the part of speech
The opposite should be usable in the same slot: the opposite of the adjective TRANSPARENT is the adjective opaque, not the noun 'opacity'. If two options both fit the meaning, prefer the one matching the part of speech.

### Do not confuse opposite with absence
The opposite must **reverse** the meaning, not merely remove it:
- For GENEROUS, 'careful' is not enough; the reverse idea is mean or stingy.
- For BRAVE, 'calm' is not the opposite; cowardly is.
Ask: does this option describe the other end of the same scale, or just a different street?

### Quick revision
- Three kinds: complementary, gradable, direction/role.
- Never flip the prefix: invaluable = very valuable; inflammable = burns easily.
- A synonym in the options is always wrong here — strike it out first.
- Match the part of speech of the stem.
- The opposite must reverse the idea, not drop it.

patterns.name: True opposite on the same scale
patterns.howToSpot: The stem and the right answer sit at the two ends of one scale; two options are unrelated words.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the scale the stem lives on (quantity, size, temperature, willingness).
2. Name the other end of the scale in plain words.
3. Pick the option that sits at that other end.

*Why it works:* antonyms are scale-mates, so fixing the scale fixes the answer.

example.solution: Scale = quantity. Other end = plenty → **plentiful**.

patterns.name: Prefix-flip false antonym
patterns.howToSpot: One option is built by flipping a prefix (flammable, valuable) and looks like the opposite of the stem.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the stem's real meaning from memory, not from its shape.
2. Check the false-flip list (invaluable, inflammable, disinterested, restive).
3. Choose the option that genuinely reverses that meaning.

*Why it works:* these words are planted exactly because their shape lies.

example.solution: Invaluable = extremely valuable → opposite **worthless**. 'Valuable' is the shape trap.

patterns.name: Strike the synonyms first
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three options mean the same as the stem (extra, surplus, spare for superfluous).
patterns.logic:
1. In an antonym question, delete every option that means the same as the stem.
2. What remains is usually one true opposite plus one unrelated word.
3. Choose the one on the same scale.

*Why it works:* examiners always seed synonym decoys; removing them halves the work.

example.solution: Extra and surplus are synonyms → strike both → **essential** remains.

patterns.name: Opposite with matching part of speech
patterns.howToSpot: Two options carry opposite ideas but different forms (opaque vs opacity; optimistic vs optimism).
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the stem's part of speech.
2. Prefer the opposite that shares it.
3. Only fall back to the other form if nothing matches.

*Why it works:* the replaced word must fit the same sentence slot.

example.solution: Verb → **descend**. Rise and climb are synonyms; they fail the meaning check first anyway.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy for vocabulary questions
subtopics.concept:
Tier 1 typically carries only 1 synonym + 1 antonym, and Tier 2 a similar sprinkle — low volume, but each is a 15-second mark with none of grammar's ambiguity. The strategy is therefore about *conversion rate*, not time.

**The conversion system:**
- **Daily 15 minutes** on the word bank in this topic: 10 words a day, meanings read aloud, each used in one sentence of your own. Production, not recognition, fixes recall.
- **Weekly mixed test:** 30 random words from the bank — synonym for half, antonym for half. Target 26+.
- **PYQ mining:** note every vocabulary word from past papers into a personal sheet; the same words return within 2–4 years.
- **Root of the day:** one root and its five relatives. Forty days completes the root table.

**In the exam:** vocabulary items should take 15–20 seconds each. If a word is unknown, split it for roots; if still dark, judge its charge (+/−) from the shape and pick a matching-charge option — this beats random guessing. There is no negative marking on one skipped item's worth of time saved, but never leave an SSC vocabulary item blank: an educated 50-50 is positive expected value, and pure instinct in English correlates surprisingly well with correctness.

**Do not sacrifice** grammar or RC time for vocabulary — the return per minute is far higher there. Vocabulary is a background process: daily small doses, permanent retention.

tricks.title: Two-pass vocabulary
tricks.body: Answer every certain vocabulary item in the first pass (15 s each); in the second pass, return to unknowns and root-split them with the remaining time.

tricks.title: Charge guess with options
tricks.body: Options reveal the axis: if options are (kind, cruel, wealthy, talkative), the axis is temperament — now guess the word's charge from its sound (mal-, dys- negative; bene-, eu- positive) and pick accordingly.

tricks.title: The 2-4 year echo
tricks.body: Words repeat across years. Solving the last 5 years' synonym/antonym questions is the single highest-yield vocabulary exercise — the bank above already encodes that history.

mistakes: Cramming 500 words the night before; retention needs spaced daily doses.
Spending five minutes on one unknown word worth one mark.
Leaving vocabulary blank instead of making an educated charge-based choice.
Learning meanings without using the word in a sentence — recognition without recall.
subtopics.notes:
### What the exam actually asks
In SSC, Railway and Banking papers, vocabulary appears in three shapes: a bare word for its synonym, a bare word for its antonym, and a word in CAPITALS inside a sentence. Tier 1 usually carries one synonym and one antonym; each is a 15-second mark with no calculation. This subtopic trains the routine that handles all three shapes.

### The 15-second routine
1. **Tone first**: say whether the word is positive, negative or neutral. This alone kills two options most of the time.
2. **Part of speech**: adjective, verb or noun — the answer must match.
3. **Root check**: if the word is unknown, try the prefix/root method.
4. **Eliminate to two**: strike the synonyms (in an antonym question) or the opposites (in a synonym question), and the unrelated word.
5. **Choose the nearest**: between the last two, pick the one closer in strength and tone, not the fancier word.

### Sentence-based items
When the word sits in a sentence, the sentence is the boss:
- Read the full sentence and paraphrase the capitalised word in one plain word.
- Then apply the same routine to your plain word, not to the printed word.
Example: *His GAUNT face showed months of illness.* Gaunt here = thin and bony; the most opposite option is plump, while thin and pale are meaning traps.

### Building the word bank
Vocabulary marks come from memory, so the plan is a bank, not brilliance:
- Add every new word from every mock test to a personal sheet with its meaning, one synonym, one antonym.
- Revise the sheet weekly; words you miss twice move to a small weak list.
- Learn words in opposite pairs (barren/fertile, scarce/plentiful, clement/harsh) — one memory slot stores two answers.
- High-frequency exam words worth banking: lucid, tenacious, vigilant, frugal, notorious, imminent, futile, mitigate, squander, abundant, indispensable.

### Guessing rules
- In a synonym question, an option that is the *opposite* of the stem is wrong; so is a word from a different class of idea.
- In an antonym question, any synonym option is wrong — strike it without reading further.
- If two options survive, the shorter plainer word is more often the keyed answer than a rare showy word.
- Never leave a vocabulary blank in exams without negative marking pressure issues — these are among the fastest questions on the paper, so bank them early and save time for grammar.

### Quick revision
- Routine: tone → part of speech → root → eliminate → nearest.
- Sentence given: paraphrase the capital word first.
- Learn in opposite pairs; keep a mock-test word sheet and revise weekly.
- Antonym question: synonyms are always wrong. Synonym question: opposites are always wrong.
- Prefer the plainer survivor over the showy one.

patterns.name: Synonym of a word inside a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence with the key word in CAPITALS; the options are possible meanings.
patterns.logic:
1. Paraphrase the capital word from the sentence's sense.
2. Apply tone and part-of-speech filters.
3. Match the paraphrase to the options.

*Why it works:* the sentence fixes the sense the examiner keyed.

example.q: *His account of the accident was COHERENT.*
example.solution: Account that hangs together → **clear and logical**.

patterns.name: Antonym of a word inside a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: Same shape as the synonym-in-sentence item but the stem asks for the most opposite option.
patterns.logic:
1. Paraphrase the capital word.
2. Strike every option that means the same as the paraphrase.
3. Choose the remaining option that truly reverses it.

*Why it works:* the synonym strike removes the planted decoys instantly.

example.q: *His GAUNT face showed months of illness.*
example.solution: Gaunt = thin and bony → most opposite **plump**.

patterns.name: Mixed drill: one stem, both directions
patterns.howToSpot: A set mixes synonym and antonym items; the habit to train is checking the direction asked before reading options.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the command word first: nearest or most opposite.
2. Only then look at the stem word and fix its tone.
3. Apply the matching strike rule (synonyms out for antonyms; opposites out for synonyms).

*Why it works:* most vocabulary errors are direction errors, not knowledge errors.

example.solution: Command = opposite → **defeated**. Triumphant and successful are synonym decoys.

patterns.name: Unknown word: root plus context together
patterns.howToSpot: The capital word is unfamiliar, but the sentence and the word's parts each give a clue.
patterns.logic:
1. Split the word for a prefix or root (aud = hear, port = carry).
2. Check the split against the sentence: does 'able to be heard' fit the slot?
3. Choose the option the two clues agree on.

*Why it works:* two weak clues pointing the same way are strong together.

example.q: *Even in the last row the lecturer's voice was AUDIBLE.*
example.solution: aud = hear → **able to be heard**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A bare capitalised word with four options; the command says 'nearest in meaning'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the word's meaning in one plain word, then run the filters in order: part of speech, class of idea, degree, charge (positive or negative). Strike options that fail any filter and pick the survivor closest in strength and tone.

example.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  LUCID
example.solution: **Clear**. Lucid writing is easy to understand; 'dull' and 'lengthy' are class mismatches.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A bare capitalised word; the command says 'most opposite'. At least one option is a synonym of the stem.
pyqPatterns.approach: Strike every synonym of the stem first — in an antonym question they are always wrong. Then name the scale the word sits on and choose the option at the other end, not merely a different word.

example.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  HUMBLE
example.solution: **Proud**. Modest would be a synonym; proud sits at the other end of the same scale.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Root-based decoding of an unfamiliar word
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem word is long or technical-looking but contains a known prefix or root (mal-, bene-, chron-, spect-, port-).
pyqPatterns.approach: Split the word into prefix + root + suffix, translate the pieces, and assemble a plain meaning. Match that meaning to the options, and check the part of speech of the ending (-ous, -tion, -ness).

example.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  TENACIOUS
example.solution: **Persistent** — tenax = holding firmly; one who holds on does not give up.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: An option built by flipping the stem's prefix (flammable, valuable, interested) seems to be the opposite.
pyqPatterns.approach: Never build the opposite by adding or removing a prefix. Recall the stem's real meaning from memory (invaluable = extremely valuable; inflammable = burns easily), then choose the option that truly reverses it.

example.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  INVALUABLE
example.solution: **Worthless**. Invaluable means priceless; 'valuable' is the shape trap that means the same, not the opposite.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Synonym or antonym of a word inside a sentence
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The key word appears in CAPITALS inside a full sentence, and the options are meanings or opposites of that use.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the whole sentence and paraphrase the capitalised word in one plain word — the context fixes which sense is being tested. Then apply the usual filters to your paraphrase, not to the printed word.

example.q: His IMMINENT arrival made everyone hurry. (nearest in meaning)
example.solution: **About to happen** — the sentence shows the arrival is just ahead, so 'overdue' and 'unexpected' fail the context.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Synonym with degree or connotation trap
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two options share the right class of idea but differ in strength or tone (serious vs vital; well known vs notorious).
pyqPatterns.approach: Place the stem word on its scale and note its charge. Extreme stems take extreme answers; negative stems take negative answers. Choose the option matching both, and reject the weaker or wrongly toned survivor.

example.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  NOTORIOUS
example.solution: **Infamous** — both are negative fame. 'Famous' has the right class but the wrong charge.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Vocabulary hidden inside cloze and fill-in items
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A cloze blank or a fill-in item whose four options are near-synonyms; the mark depends on vocabulary plus context.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the tone and part of speech the sentence needs, remove options of the wrong charge or form, then test the survivors in the blank. Choose the one that collocates naturally with the surrounding words.

example.q: Fill in: *The chairman's speech was ___ and everyone understood the plan.* (lucid / illegal / lucidly / limp)
example.solution: **Lucid** — an adjective is needed before the noun, and 'understood the plan' confirms the clear sense.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A run of items alternates between 'nearest in meaning' and 'most opposite' for the same word bank.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the command word before the stem and say the required direction aloud (same or reverse). Apply the matching strike rule: synonyms are wrong for opposites, opposites are wrong for synonyms. Most errors here are direction errors, not knowledge errors.

example.solution: **Dense**. Thinly scattered is the meaning — a synonym decoy — while dense sits at the other end of the same scale.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

BENEVOLENT
solvedExamples.solution: *Benevolent* = bene (good) + vol (wishing) = wishing others well → **compassionate**. The root instantly disposes of *malevolent* (male- = bad), which is its antonym and a planted decoy; *miserly* is about money and *talkative* about speech.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Split the word: bene- = good → pick the warm option; the male- option is the trap.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

FRUGAL
solvedExamples.solution: *Frugal* means careful and sparing with money → **thrifty**. *Lavish* is its direct opposite (spending freely), and the other two are topic-shifters. Degree also confirms it: both 'frugal' and 'thrifty' sit at the same moderate mark of careful spending.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Meaning in your words ('spends carefully') → match, then check that the strongest-sounding option is not the antonym.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

CORDIAL
solvedExamples.solution: *Cordial* = warm and friendly. The genuine contradiction is **hostile**. *Polite* and *sincere* both coexist with cordiality (a cordial host is also polite), so neither opposes it; *formal* describes style, not warmth.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mini-sentence test: 'a cordial welcome' vs 'a ___ welcome' — only one option truly flips the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

ABUNDANT
practice.solution: *Abundant* = existing in more than enough quantity → **plentiful**. *Scarce* is its antonym and is planted first-position bait; 'hidden' and 'tiny' shift to other dimensions altogether.
practice.shortcut: Own words first ('more than enough') → match.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

FUTILE
practice.solution: *Futile* = producing no result → **pointless**. 'Useful' is the opposite pole; 'fertile' and 'fragile' share the -ile ending to punish shape-readers.
practice.shortcut: Kill same-suffix decoys, keep the meaning match.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

IMMINENT
practice.solution: *Imminent* = about to happen at any moment → **impending**. 'Delayed/distant' push the event away in time — the opposite direction.
practice.shortcut: Time word: 'about to happen' → pick the option meaning 'on its way'.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

NOTORIOUS
practice.solution: *Notorious* is famous **for bad reasons** → **infamous**. 'Renowned/celebrated/popular' all carry a positive charge — the charge mismatch is the entire test here.
practice.shortcut: Charge matching: a negative word needs a negative option.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

INDISPENSABLE
practice.solution: *Indispensable* = too necessary to do without → **essential**. 'Optional' flips the meaning; the others shift axes. Prefix logic agrees: in- (not) + dispensable (able to be let go).
practice.shortcut: Prefix flip: not dispensable → must be kept → essential.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

MITIGATE
practice.solution: *Mitigate* = soften the severity of something → **lessen**. *Aggravate* is the planted antonym; 'prolong' and 'conceal' change the action, not its intensity.
practice.shortcut: Root family: mit/miss (send) — 'send away the severity' → lessen.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

VIGILANT
practice.solution: *Vigilant* = carefully watchful for danger → **alert**. 'Careless' and 'drowsy' are opposite-directed; 'hostile' shifts to temperament.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

SQUANDER
practice.solution: *Squander* = spend or use carelessly → **waste**. 'Save' is its opposite; 'donate' is controlled giving, not waste; 'multiply' changes the direction entirely.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

TENACIOUS
practice.solution: *Tenacious* = holding on firmly, refusing to quit → **persistent**. 'Fragile' and 'sluggish' are the planted opposite-temperament options.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

LUCID
practice.solution: *Lucid* = easy to understand, transparent in expression → **clear**. 'Murky' is the opposite direction; 'lengthy/loud' are sound-shape decoys sharing the u-c sound.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

HUMBLE
practice.solution: *Humble* = modest about one's worth. The genuine opposite is **proud**. 'Modest' is a synonym planted as bait; 'gentle/polite' describe manner, not self-regard.
practice.shortcut: Mini-sentence: 'a humble officer' vs 'a ___ officer' — only one option truly inverts it.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

PUNCTUAL
practice.solution: *Punctual* = exactly on time. Its opposite is **late**. 'Early' is not the opposite — arriving early is still not punctual in the strict sense, and SSC's key follows 'late'; 'prompt/regular' are near-synonyms.
practice.shortcut: Time-axis test: on time ↔ behind time.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

TRANSPARENT
practice.solution: *Transparent* = letting light through; its standard opposite is **opaque**. 'Visible/lucid' move in a different dimension; 'brittle' is physical weakness.
practice.shortcut: Physical sense here: see-through ↔ not see-through.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

LIBERTY
practice.solution: *Liberty* = freedom from restraint → opposite **bondage**. 'Freedom' is the synonym bait; 'licence' is unrestrained permission, not captivity; 'leisure' is free time.
practice.shortcut: The synonym is always the first option to kill in antonym questions.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

VIRTUE
practice.solution: *Virtue* = moral goodness → its standard opposite is **vice** (moral fault). 'Value' drifts to worth, and the v-initial 'virtuosity/vigour' are shape decoys.
practice.shortcut: Kill the v-initial decoys; pick the genuine moral opposite.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  MALICIOUS
practice.solution: mal = bad → intending harm → **spiteful**. The other options fail the direction check: a mal- word must be negative.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  MAGNANIMOUS
practice.solution: magn (great) + anim (mind, spirit) → great-spirited = **generous**, ready to forgive. Miserly is the opposite direction.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  AMICABLE
practice.solution: am/amic = friend (as in amiable) → **friendly**. An amicable settlement is a friendly one; hostile fails the direction check.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  PORTABLE
practice.solution: port = carry → **easy to carry** (transport, export share the root).

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  BENEFACTOR
options: one who gives money or help
practice.solution: bene = good + factor (doer) → one who does good = **one who gives money or help**. The direction check removes everything negative.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  INSPECT
practice.solution: spect = look → to look into = **examine closely** (spectator, spectacle share the root).

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  CHRONOLOGICAL
practice.solution: chron = time → **arranged in time order** (a chronology of events).

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  RESTIVE
practice.solution: **Restive** = restless, hard to control. It merely looks like 'rest' — a false-root word, so 'calm' is the trap.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  ENERVATE
practice.solution: **Enervate** = to drain of strength = weaken. It looks like 'energy' but points the other way; 'energise' is the planted trap.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  CIRCUMVENT
options: to get around by clever means
practice.solution: circum = around + vent = come → to come around a rule = **get around it by clever means**.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  TRIVIAL
practice.solution: **Trivial** = of very little importance. Serious and vital sit at the wrong end of the importance scale.
practice.shortcut: Degree: trivial is the low end.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  HOSTILE
practice.solution: **Hostile** = showing enmity → unfriendly. The charge must stay negative.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  DELUGE
practice.solution: **Deluge** = a great flood of water — the extreme end. Drizzle, drought and mist are the same class but the wrong degree.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  RELEASE
practice.solution: The stem is a verb, so **set free** matches the slot; 'freedom' is the noun decoy; capture and tighten reverse the meaning.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  ABOLISH
practice.solution: **Abolish** = to do away with (a law, a system) — a verb; 'establish' is its opposite.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  CAUTIOUS
practice.solution: **Cautious** = careful to avoid danger. Careless, bold and hasty carry the opposite charge.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

His LACONIC reply contained exactly two words.
practice.solution: A two-word reply → **using very few words**. The sentence fixes the sense; lengthy and talkative point the other way.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The new medicine ALLEVIATED the patient's pain within an hour.
practice.solution: A medicine that helps within an hour → **lessened** the pain. Increased and caused reverse the sense.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  SCARCE
practice.solution: Scale = quantity. The far end of scarce is **plentiful**; tiny, weak and short are unrelated scales.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  ACCEPT
practice.solution: Complementary pair: accept ↔ **refuse**. 'Except' only looks like 'accept' — a spelling trap, not an opposite.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  INVALUABLE
practice.solution: **Invaluable** = extremely valuable (priceless), so its true opposite is **worthless**. Priceless, expensive and valuable are all synonym traps built on the prefix flip.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  INFLAMMABLE
practice.solution: **Inflammable** = easily set on fire (the same as flammable), so the opposite is **fireproof**. Flammable is the famous false-flip trap.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  SUPERFLUOUS
practice.solution: **Superfluous** = more than needed. Surplus, extra and spare all mean the same — strike the synonyms first; what truly reverses it is **essential**.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  MAXIMUM
practice.solution: Scale = amount. The other end of maximum is **minimum**; the other three are synonyms.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  OPTIMIST
practice.solution: The -ist nouns pair up: optimist ↔ **pessimist**. A realist and an idealist differ in outlook but are not opposites of an optimist.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  ASCEND
practice.solution: Direction pair: ascend ↔ **descend**. Climb, rise and mount are synonym decoys.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The old tractor was still SERVICEABLE after twenty years.
practice.solution: Still working after twenty years → **fit for use**. The sentence, not the word's rarity, decides.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The witness gave a clear and COHERENT account of the accident.
practice.solution: An account that hangs together → **logical and connected**. Confusing points the other way; brief and false are different ideas altogether.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

In the dry summer the fields lay BARREN.
practice.solution: **Barren** = bearing no crop; its true opposite is **fertile**. Dry, empty and bare all mean the same as barren — strike the synonyms first.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The judge was known for his CLEMENT decisions.
practice.solution: **Clement** = mild, merciful. Gentle, mild and forgiving are synonyms; the reverse of mercy is **harsh**.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  ECONOMICAL
practice.solution: **Economical** = avoiding waste → careful with money. Extravagant is the opposite charge.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  VICTORIOUS
practice.solution: Command word = opposite. Strike the synonym decoys (triumphant, winning, successful) → **defeated**.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

Even in the last row the lecturer's voice was clearly AUDIBLE.
practice.solution: aud = hear, and the sentence confirms it → **able to be heard**. Root and context point the same way.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The hill village had a SPARSE population scattered over many slopes.
practice.solution: Scattered over many slopes → **thinly scattered**. Dense is the opposite; the other two are unrelated.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  AMATEUR
practice.solution: **Amateur** = one who plays for pleasure, not pay → non-professional. Expert, professional and skilled all point the other way.

practice.q:
Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

The injection had an IMMEDIATE effect on the fever.
practice.solution: Effect right after the injection → **instant**. Delayed is the opposite; sudden means unexpected, brief means short — different ideas.

practice.q: Select the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.  PROPOSED
practice.solution: **Proposed** = put forward (a plan, a name). Rejected, withdrawn and opposed reverse or block the act.

practice.q:
Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the word in CAPITALS.

His GAUNT face showed the months he had spent in hospital.
practice.solution: **Gaunt** = thin and bony. Thin and haggard are synonym decoys; pale is a different idea; the true opposite is **plump**.

practice.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  ABANDON
practice.solution: Desert, forsake and quit all mean the same as **abandon** — strike the synonyms first; the word that truly reverses it is **retain** (to keep).
